keyVerseText: Then saith Jesus unto them, All ye shall be offended because of me this night: for it is written, I will smite the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered abroad.
rootMeaning: The Greek word ποίμνη (poímnē) derives from the verb ποιμαίνω (poimaínō), which means to feed or to rule, especially in the sense of tending sheep. This root highlights the literal action of shepherding—caring for and guiding a flock. Thus, ποίμνη carries the sense not merely of a group of animals but of those under the watchful care and governance of a shepherd, enriching the common English gloss of 'flock' with the nuance of pastoral oversight and protection.
usageInScripture: The word ποίμνη appears five times in Scripture, consistently translated as 'flock,' 'a flock,' or 'fold.' This consistency underscores its primary literal meaning of a group of sheep or animals. However, it also carries metaphorical weight, referring to people as a flock under spiritual care, as noted in its use to describe Christ's followers. The translations reveal a stable semantic range emphasizing a collective under shepherdly care, whether literal or figurative.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ποίμνη in its original sense deepens our grasp of the shepherd-flock relationship central to biblical theology. It reminds believers that Christ, the Good Shepherd, exercises loving oversight and protection over His people. This term conveys not only belonging but also the responsibility of care and guidance inherent in pastoral ministry. Recognizing the flock as those tenderly tended by Christ enriches our appreciation of His sacrificial leadership and the intimate bond between the Savior and His followers.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 26:31, Jesus foretells that the sheep of the flock will be scattered when the shepherd is struck. The use of ποίμνη here emphasizes the vulnerability and dependence of the followers on their shepherd. This term highlights the intimate relationship between Christ and His people, underscoring the seriousness of His impending suffering and the temporary disarray it will cause among His followers. It invites reflection on the shepherd's role and the eventual restoration of the scattered flock.
